claims.text: Ahpra and the National Boards (including the Psychology Board of Australia) published principles for the safe use of AI in healthcare (August 2024), placing responsibility on the registered practitioner for verifying AI-generated content, maintaining contemporaneous records, and obtaining patient consent before AI-assisted documentation. The Psychology Board's refreshed Code of Conduct (2025) and Professional Competencies for Psychologists (effective 1 December 2025) embed digital-competence expectations for AI use.

claims.text: Jobs and Skills Australia's 'Our Gen AI Transition' Capacity Study (August 2025) scores occupations on augmentability and automatability (0-1, ILO-adapted) across 358 occupations; it finds augmentation outweighs automation economy-wide and that knowledge-intensive professional roles at ANZSCO Skill Levels 1-2 show the highest augmentation exposure. This occupation is a professional Skill Level 1 role, placing it in the high-augmentation, low-automation band.

claims.text: A 2026 narrative review of AI in psychological practice reports unintended consequences for psychologists themselves: cognitive offloading and automation bias can erode diagnostic reasoning and clinical judgement, while moral deskilling, technostress, data dependence and vendor lock-in threaten practitioner wellbeing and professional sovereignty. The authors frame the central risk as a 'competence paradox' - mistaking fluent tool use for understanding.
